texts.text: ABSTRACT

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer among women globally and a significant public health challenge in China, which accounts for nearly 18% of global cervical cancer cases. The HPV vaccine is a proven intervention for preventing high-risk HPV infections and associated cancers. This serial crosssectional study conducted in Shanghai, China, in 2019 and 2024 analyzed changes in HPV vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess the associations between HPV vaccination, general vaccine hesitancy, and HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy, adjusting for sociodemographic factors. The Population Attributable Fraction (PAF) quantified the proportion of nonvaccination attributable to these factors. In 2019 and 2024, two waves of data were collected from 1,037 and 1,450 parents, respectively. Results showed an increase in HPV vaccination from 6% to 30% during the study period, primarily among women aged 18 and older, while coverage among the WHO target group (girls aged 9–14) remained low at 8%. Parents with HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy were 75% less likely to vaccinate their daughters (OR = 0.25, 95% CI: 0.11–0.56), while general vaccine hesitancy reduced vaccination likelihood by 94% (OR = 0.06, 95% CI: 0.00–0.89). PAF analysis indicated that HPVspecific vaccine hesitancy contributed to 24% of non-vaccination cases, higher than general vaccine hesitancy (10%). These findings highlight the critical need for targeted interventions addressing HPVspecific barriers, improving education about vaccination timing and options, and reducing logistical obstacles to align with global cervical cancer elimination goals.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer among women globally, with an estimated 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths in 2020. 1 The Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine has long been proven to provide effective protection against high-risk HPV strains, including those which cause cervical and other cancers. To decrease this burden, the World Health Organization (WHO) has set a target of ensuring 90% of girls are fully vaccinated with the HPV vaccine by age 15 as part of a global effort to eliminate cervical cancer. 2 Despite its proven effectiveness, significant disparities persist in vaccine access and uptake. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) adopted the vaccine later than high-income countrieswith approximately 144 countries now including the HPV vaccine in their national immunization programs (NIPs). This comprises over 98% of high-income countries, but only 46% of low-income and 59% of lower-middle-income countries. 3 Rapid roll-out of HPV vaccination in LMICs is essential to narrow these inequalities and reduce the global burden of HPV-related diseases.

texts.orig: Unlike general vaccine hesitancy, which broadly includes mistrust in healthcare systems, fear of side effects, and misinformation, 11 HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy includes barriers unique to that vaccine. These impediments involve cultural stigma associated with a sexually transmitted infection (STI), low awareness of HPV-related cancer risks, and misconceptions that vaccination promotes early sexual activity. 12 , 13 Differentiating between general vaccine hesitancy and HPVspecific vaccine hesitancy is crucial for designing targeted public health interventions. 14 This distinction enables tailored strate -gies to address the root causes of resistance, optimize resource allocation, and ultimately increase vaccination uptake to prevent cervical cancer.

The study aims to: (1) assess changes in parents' acceptance of the HPV vaccine for their children between 2019 and 2024, (2) examine the associations between HPV vaccination, general vaccine hesitancy, and HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy, and (3) quantify the proportion of nonvaccination attributable to general and HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy. texts.label: text
texts.orig: This study used a two-wave cross-sectional design to assess trends in HPV vaccination uptake, vaccine hesitancy, and parental acceptance in Shanghai, China. The first wave of data collection occurred in 2019, followed by a second wave in 2024. Both surveys collected information on general and HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy, HPV vaccination status, willingness to vaccinate, and sociodemographic characteristics. By comparing data across the two time points and applying regression models and population attributable fraction analyses, we evaluated changes over time and quantified the impact of hesitancy on HPV vaccination outcomes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The first wave of data collection took place in Shanghai, China, between May and July 2019. The sampling method has been detailed elsewhere. 15 Briefly, all districts in Shanghai, except Chongming Island – a less-populated island distant from the city – were included in the study. Forty townships were selected based on population size, as determined by the 2010 Census. Within each township, parents were randomly selected from immunization clinics, elementary schools, middle schools, and high schools to create a comprehensive sample representing children of all ages. Parents with at least one child aged ≤18 years were eligible to participate.

texts.orig: General vaccine hesitancy was assessed using the Parent Attitudes About Childhood Vaccines (PACV) scale, which includes three subdomains: general attitudes, safety and efficacy, and behavior. Details of the assessment and categorization of vaccine hesitancy have been previously published. 15 Briefly, responses to questions were scored as "hesitant" (scored as 2), "not sure/don't know" (scored as 1), or "not hesitant" (scored as 0). Scores were summed and converted to a 0–100 scale, with scores < 50 categorized as "not hesitant" and ≥ 50 as "hesitant." A similar scoring system was applied to the subdomains.

texts.text: Discussion

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In our serial cross-sectional study conducted in 2019 and 2024 in Shanghai, China, a significant increase in HPV vaccination among girls was observed over the 5 years, climbing from 6% to 30%, particularly among those aged 18 and older. This increase aligns with parents' acceptance of the vaccine when asked in the context of hypothetical children. However, while overall acceptance improved, acceptance for the younger age group decreased. That means the increased vaccination rate mostly come from the older age group children. Our analysis further confirmed that older age is significantly associated with higher HPV vaccination rates. We also found that HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy accounted for about 24% of HPV non-vaccination, suggesting that eliminating HPV-specific hesitancy could substantially reduce non-vaccination rates.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Since initial HPV vaccine approval in 2016, China has made notable progress in increasing vaccination coverage through policy changes, domestic vaccine production, and public health initiatives. These efforts have addressed key barriers such as cost, awareness, and accessibility to better align with global cervical cancer elimination goals. Although parental knowledge of HPV has improved from 51% to 67% in our study, HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy remains high at 28%, indicating that knowledge alone may not be sufficient to shift attitudes and actions. Additional challenges such as uneven vaccine distribution, competing health priorities, and persistent misinformation continue to hinder the vaccine uptake, highlighting the need for targeted behavioral and communication strategies along with the structural improvements. 16

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Although overall HPV vaccination coverage has increased, most recipients are young adults aged 18 and older, while vaccination coverage for girls aged 9–14 remains very low. This finding is consistent with other studies across China. a study in Shenzhen, a developed southern city, reported that 23% of women aged 18–26 received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine, while coverage for girls aged 9–17 was less than 5%. 17 National data also indicates that coverage among the WHO target age group of 9–14 years was only 4%, 8 far below the rates in Japan (26%), South Africa (49%), and the United States (80%), and significantly short of the 90% target set by WHO. 18

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Our findings indicate that the lower coverage for younger age groups may result from vaccine supply constraints, limited-service accessibility, high vaccine costs, and insufficient awareness about the optimal timing for vaccination. 19 In the past, HPV vaccines in China were primarily recommended for adult women due to limited supply and age restrictions. 19 For instance, the bivalent HPV vaccine was restricted to females aged 9–25 before 2018, the quadrivalent vaccine was only available for ages 20–40 years before 2019. The nonavalent vaccine (protect against nine different HPV serotypes) was limited to ages 16–26 years before 2021. 8 In 2022, vaccine eligibility was expanded to include women aged 9–45 years. The quadrivalent vaccine was approved for men 9–26 in January 2025. However, a lack of clear understanding about the different vaccine types among the public continues to hinder informed decision-making. 16 An over-preference for the nonavalent vaccine has created supply shortages, making it difficult for individuals to access to the vaccine. 20 A study involving over 4,000 eligible parents in China showed that among those intending to vaccinate their daughters, 62% attempted to schedule a vaccination appointment, but only 16% succeeded. 20 These persistent challenges have led some women to pay extra for vaccination at private clinics or turn to scalpers, who resell vaccine slots at inflated prices. 21 This "scalping" phenomenon has contributed to frustration and distrust, which may translate into hesitancy or even abandoning plans for vaccination. Thus, these structural constrains not only limit physical access but also reinforce psychological barriers to vaccine acceptance. Besides increasing the vaccine supply, objective education about vaccine choices, consistent updates on government funding policies, and sustained improvements in public health services are needed to address these challenges.

texts.orig: Our PAF analysis showed that general vaccine hesitancy accounted for 10% of HPV non-vaccination, while HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy contributed 24%. General vaccine hesitancy involves issues such as medical mistrust, exposure to misinformation about vaccines, and concerns about safety and efficacy. 22 HPV-specific hesitancy, however, includes unique barriers such as stigma associated with HPV as an STI, low awareness of the link between HPV and cancer, and cultural factors such as gender norms, taboos around sex and STIs and religious beliefs. 12 , 13 These findings align with studies conducted in other countries, such as the United States, where parental hesitancy for the HPV vaccine was found to be about four times higher than for other childhood vaccines. 23 HPV-specific concerns include fears of vaccine novelty, 23 potential serious side effects (e.g., vaginal bleeding), 24 myths about a link to infertility, and worries that vaccination may encourage sexual activity (so called, sexual disinhibition). 25 Our earlier study demonstrated that framing the HPV vaccine as a cancer-prevention tool and providing information about its role in preventing sexually transmitted infections improved parents' acceptance. 15 These results emphasize the importance of addressing HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy through tailored interventions. Future research should focus on under -standing specific barriers in greater detail and developing messaging that reframes the HPV vaccine as a tool for preventing multiple types of cancer.

texts.orig: To improve HPV vaccination uptake among girls aged 9–14, several actionable strategies can be implemented in response to our findings. First, school-based vaccination programs have been effective in many countries, as they reach adolescents in a structured and accessible setting, thus reducing logistical barriers for families. A nationwide study in France evaluating various interventions to improve HPV vaccination rate found that school-based programs were the only approach that consistently and significantly increased vaccination coverage, even after the trial ended. 26 Second, parental education sessions held during school meetings delivered by healthcare providers using tailored messaging are essential for addressing misinformation about HPV and the vaccine. This can help with clarifying differences between vaccine types, potential side effects and empowering parents to make informed decisions. Lastly, up-to-date information about reimbursement policies and vaccine availability should be communicated to parents regularly to reduce cost-related hesitancy and encourage timely vaccination.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There are strengths and limitations to our study. The serial cross-sectional design allowed us to observe changes in parental attitudes over time and assess the impact of new policies to promote the HPV vaccine. Matching the 2019 and 2024 datasets on key socioeconomic variables enhanced comparability. Additionally, the PAF analysis quantified the contribution of general and HPV-specific vaccine hesitancy to nonvaccination, helping prioritize strategies for promoting vaccination. However, as a cross-sectional study, it is subject to unmeasured confounding and imprecise measurements, limiting causal inferences. The PAF estimates are approximations and may not fully capture the complex associations between non-vaccination and hesitancy factors. Residual confounding may also persist despite matching efforts.
